summary: Mercian noblewoman who married Alfred the Great in 868 and bore Edward the Elder and Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians; never styled queen, she founded the Nunnaminster at Winchester as a widow.
overview: Ealhswith, a Mercian noblewoman of royal descent, married Alfred of Wessex in 868 and bore him five children who grew up, among them Edward the Elder and Æthelflæd. West Saxon custom denied her the title of queen, and she is best remembered for founding the Nunnaminster, a nunnery at Winchester, after Alfred's death.
greatestFeats: Mother of Edward the Elder and of Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians

keyAchievements: Wife of Alfred the Great from 868 to 899

birth.note: No source records her birth; she was presumably young when she married in 868.

death.circumstance: Her death is recorded without a cause; she was buried in the New Minster at Winchester, the abbey her son completed.

quickFacts.knownFor: Marriage to Alfred the Great and founding the Nunnaminster at Winchester

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Ealhswith was the wife of Alfred the Great for thirty-one years, from their marriage in 868 until his death in 899. Her father was Æthelred Mucel, ealdorman of the Gaini, an old Mercian tribal people, and her mother Eadburh came from the Mercian royal family, so the match joined the West Saxon royal house to Mercian royal blood at a time when Danish armies were overrunning both kingdoms.

She was never crowned or called queen, and the writers of Alfred's reign barely mention her. Her importance lies in her children, above all Edward the Elder, king of the Anglo-Saxons, and Æthelflæd, who ruled Mercia after her husband's death, and in the Nunnaminster, the nunnery of Saint Mary at Winchester that she founded as a widow and that lasted until 1539.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Nothing is recorded of Ealhswith's birth or childhood. A charter of 897 setting out her brother's duties towards the monastery of Winchcombe, a house claimed by the family of the Mercian kings Coenwulf and Ceolwulf, led the historian Barbara Yorke to suggest that she belonged to that royal kindred, and Richard Abels goes further, making her a descendant of King Coenwulf. She married Alfred in Mercia in 868, the year a Danish army seized Nottingham. Alfred's elder brother Æthelred I of Wessex was then king, and the marriage strengthened his alliance with the Mercian king Burgred, who had already married their sister. Asser, Alfred's Welsh biographer, says the bridegroom was struck by a sudden and painful illness at the wedding feast, which had gone on day and night.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Almost nothing survives that describes Ealhswith as a person. Asser, writing in 893 while she was alive and at court, never gives her name: he calls her only Alfred's wife, of a noble Mercian family, and spends more words on her mother Eadburh, whom he says he often saw, a venerable woman who lived for many years as a chaste widow. Alfred's will, drawn up in the 880s, names Ealhswith last among its beneficiaries, leaving her the estates of Lambourn, Wantage and Edington and a hundred pounds.

Her low profile probably owes more to custom than to temperament. Asser explains that the West Saxons refused their kings' wives the name of queen because of an earlier Eadburh, a daughter of King Offa of Mercia, who was said to have poisoned King Beorhtric of Wessex by mistake in 802. Her actions as a widow show means and purpose: she witnessed a charter of 901 as Ealhswið mater regis, placed straight after her son and ahead of his wife, and she founded a religious house of her own. Two early tenth-century manuscripts call her the English people's true and dear lady, a formal tribute rather than a portrait.

contentSections.title: Marriage to Alfred
paragraphs: Ealhswith's married life coincided with the worst years of the Viking wars. Alfred became king in 871, and after a Danish surprise attack in the winter of 878 he was driven into the marshes of Somerset before his victory at the Battle of Edington that spring. Where Ealhswith and her young children spent those months is not recorded. Five of their children grew up: Æthelflæd, who married Æthelred, Lord of the Mercians; Edward, born around 874; Æthelgifu, whom Alfred made abbess of his new nunnery at Shaftesbury; Ælfthryth, who married the Flemish count Baldwin; and Æthelweard, whom Asser describes being taught to read at the court school alongside the sons of noblemen.

contentSections.title: Widowhood and the Nunnaminster
paragraphs: Alfred died on 26 October 899. Ealhswith kept the three estates of his will, all places tied to his memory: Wantage was his birthplace, Edington the scene of his great victory and Lambourn lay near the site of another. Edward the Elder's accession did not push her aside, and in 901 she witnessed his charter as mother of the king.

Between 899 and 902 she founded the nunnery of Saint Mary at Winchester, known as the Nunnaminster. The New Minster Liber Vitae names her as its builder, and her son completed the first buildings; his daughter Eadburh, later venerated as a saint, was among its early nuns. The nunnery stood a few hundred metres from the Old Minster and from the New Minster that Edward was building to house his father's tomb. The Book of Nunnaminster, a Mercian prayer book of the ninth century whose prayers often use feminine forms, probably belonged to Ealhswith before it passed to her community.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Ealhswith died on 5 December 902 and was buried in the New Minster at Winchester, where Edward had moved Alfred's body from the Old Minster. In 1110 the New Minster community moved to a new abbey at Hyde, just outside the city walls, and took the royal remains with them. Hyde Abbey was dissolved in 1538 and its church pulled down, and although excavations at the site have recovered human bones, none has been identified as hers.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Ealhswith's children carried West Saxon power into Mercia and the Danish-held midlands: Edward the Elder and Æthelflæd conquered the southern Danelaw between them, and her grandson Æthelstan became the first king to rule all the English. Her daughter Ælfthryth's marriage made her an ancestor of the later counts of Flanders and so of Matilda, the wife of William the Conqueror. The Nunnaminster outlived the Viking age, was reformed under Bishop Æthelwold after 963 and was suppressed in the Dissolution of the Monasteries in November 1539. Part of its excavated site is now laid out beside Abbey Passage in Winchester.
